title: Formal occasions
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedTenses: presente, L1-M6's, which is where a formula is delivered
the passive with essere plus a participle: è stato, è stata
the passive with venire, present only: viene consegnato
condizionale of politeness in one lexeme, vorrei, L1-M3's

rules.text: THE PASSIVE, AT LAST, AND IT HAS TWO AUXILIARIES. essere plus a past participle states a completed event or the state it left behind: il premio è stato consegnato. venire plus the same participle stages it as a PROCESS, and that is the ceremonial one: il premio viene consegnato. The participle agrees with the subject under both — premiato for a man, premiata for a woman — so a passive sentence carries two agreements, not one.

VENIRE CANNOT FORM THE COMPOUND TENSES, AND THAT LIMIT IS THE WHOLE DIFFICULTY. viene consegnato is a sentence; è venuto consegnato is not one, and no Italian will repair it for you because there is nothing there to repair. Anywhere you want a past passive, essere is the only auxiliary there is: è stato consegnato. venire's passive lives in the present and the future and nowhere else.

THE FORMULAS ARE LEARNED WHOLE AND NEVER ASSEMBLED. auguri, congratulazioni, condoglianze, un brindisi, cin cin, alla salute, evviva. Each is a fixed noise fitted to one occasion; none of them is built out of its parts at the moment of saying it, and a formula improvised on the spot is heard as an improvisation.

ENGLISH CONGRATULATIONS SPLITS IN TWO AND THE SEAM IS TIME. auguri is for what is still ahead of you — a wedding, a birthday, a new job, a journey. congratulazioni is for what you have already pulled off — a degree, a prize, a promotion. To a bride and groom it is AUGURI, because the marriage is in front of them, and congratulazioni to a couple is precisely the error an English speaker makes.

CONDOLENCES ARE FORMULAIC HERE, AND IMPROVISING READS AS CARELESS. English rewards you for finding your own words at a funeral; Italian expects le mie sentite condoglianze, and the sincerity is carried by saying the right thing rather than a new thing. Beside it, for somebody you are close to, ti sono vicino — L2-M4's vicino doing the warm half of the work.

THE CONNECTIVES AND THE OPENINGS OF A SPEECH BELONG TO WRITING. poiché for since, pertanto for therefore, inoltre for furthermore: they are what a prepared text sounds like and they would be strange across a table. Egregio opens a formal letter to one person and carissimi a warm one to several. A spoken toast, by contrast, is two words: cin cin.

sentences.display: Auguri di cuore! Evviva gli sposi!
sentences.cue: Warmest wishes! Long live the newlyweds!
sentences.literal: Wishes of heart! Hurrah the spouses!

words.note: Wishes for what is still ahead: a wedding, a birthday, a journey. Plural in form and never singular, and it is what you say to a bride and groom.
Added to a formula to warm it. Literally of heart: Italian says it with di where English says from.
A cheer raised to somebody, from e viva welded into one word. It takes a noun straight after it and no verb at all.
The couple on the day, taken as a pair. gli sposi is the two of them together; the singular names one of them.

sentences.trap: auguri, not congratulazioni. The marriage is in front of them, and Italian sorts these two words by whether the thing has happened yet.
sentences.sound: ow-GOO-ree, three syllables and the au is one of them. ev-VEE-va, with the double v held.

variations.changed: the cheer alone, raised at the table

mistake.why: congratulazioni is for what is already done. A wedding is the beginning of the thing being wished for, so the word is auguri.

sentences.usage: At a wedding, raising a glass or signing the card.
sentences.mnemonic: auguri looks forward; congratulazioni looks back.

sentences.display: Congratulazioni per il premio; inoltre, è un grande onore
sentences.cue: Congratulations on the prize; and what is more, it is a great honour
sentences.literal: Congratulations for the prize; furthermore, is a great honour

words.note: For something already achieved: a prize, a degree, a promotion. Plural like auguri, and the two are never interchangeable.
A prize or an award. The verb behind it, premiare, gives premiato and premiata — the participle this module's passive uses.
A written connective adding a second point. In conversation it sounds like a prepared text, which is exactly where it belongs.
Masculine despite the -e ending, so un grande onore. It is the word a speech reaches for when thanking the room.

sentences.trap: per, not su. Italian congratulates FOR the thing, so congratulazioni sul premio is the English preposition wearing Italian clothes.
sentences.sound: con-gra-tu-la-TSYO-nee: six syllables, and the zi is ts. o-NO-re, stress in the middle.

variations.changed: alone, which is how it is usually said
the second half alone, as a reply

mistake.why: The prize has been won. auguri wishes you well for what is coming; something already achieved takes congratulazioni.

sentences.usage: A prize-giving, a graduation, a promotion — spoken, or written on the card.

sentences.display: Le mie sentite condoglianze, ti sono vicino
sentences.cue: My heartfelt condolences, I am here for you
sentences.literal: The my felt condolences, to-you I-am near

words.note: Plural only, and formulaic: le mie sentite condoglianze is the whole thing, with sentite meaning deeply felt rather than heard.

sentences.trap: Do not improvise. English rewards finding your own words at a funeral; Italian expects the formula, and a fresh sentence reads as not knowing what to say.
sentences.sound: con-do-LYAN-tse: the gli is the ly of million, and the ze is ts.

variations.changed: without sentite, which is the shorter formula
the two words a card carries
the warm half alone, for somebody you know well

mistake.why: The word has no singular in use. It is condoglianze, plural, and the possessive in front of it is le mie.

sentences.usage: Said at a funeral, or written in a message to somebody who has lost a family member.
sentences.mnemonic: Grief takes the plural and the fixed words.

words.note: The toast itself, as a thing you make: fare un brindisi. Same form singular and plural, like every noun that ends in unstressed -i.
The clink of two glasses, said as they go up. Two words, always doubled, and never written as one.

sentences.trap: An Italian spoken toast is two words. The English instinct to make a short speech belongs to the written brindisi, not to the moment the glasses meet.
sentences.sound: BRIN-dee-see, stress on the first syllable. chin CHIN, both syllables as in the English chin.

variations.changed: the noun alone, as a proposal
the clink alone, which is its usual size

mistake.why: cin cin is not a noun and takes no article. It is the noise you make with the glass; the thing you make is un brindisi.

sentences.usage: At the table, when somebody stands up or the glasses come together.
sentences.mnemonic: You make a brindisi and you say cin cin.

sentences.cue: Let's drink to good health, cheers!

words.note: The we form of brindare, used as an invitation. It takes a: you toast TO something, never toast the thing itself.
The stock thing to toast to, learned whole. salute on its own is also what you say when somebody sneezes.

sentences.trap: alla, not a. What is toasted takes the definite article welded onto the preposition, which is why it is alla salute and never a salute.
sentences.sound: brin-DYA-mo. al-la sa-LOO-te, with the double l held and the final e sounded.

variations.changed: the toast alone, which is a whole utterance

mistake.why: brindare needs its a. Without it health becomes the direct object, and you are toasting health rather than drinking to it.

sentences.usage: Raising a glass at a table, formal or not.
sentences.mnemonic: Toast TO something: brindare takes a.

sentences.display: Il premio viene consegnato oggi, pertanto brindiamo
sentences.cue: The prize is presented today, so let's raise a glass
sentences.literal: The prize comes handed-over today, therefore we-toast

words.note: The third person of venire, first taught at L4-M5. With a participle after it, it stages a passive as a process rather than a result.
The past participle of consegnare. It agrees with the subject of the passive: consegnato for il premio, consegnata for una medaglia.
A written connective drawing a conclusion. Like inoltre it belongs to a prepared speech and would be odd across a table.

sentences.trap: venire cannot go into a compound tense. viene consegnato is a sentence; è venuto consegnato is not one, and a past passive must switch to essere.
sentences.sound: VYEH-ne. con-se-NYA-to: the gn is the ny of canyon.

variations.changed: without the day or the conclusion
the same event in the past, where essere is the only auxiliary

mistake.why: This is the sentence the rule exists to stop. venire builds no compound passive at all, so the past of viene consegnato is è stato consegnato.

sentences.usage: A programme, an announcement, a ceremony under way.
sentences.mnemonic: venire stages the handing over; essere reports it done.

sentences.display: Mia madre è stata premiata ieri
sentences.cue: My mother was given the award yesterday
sentences.literal: My mother is been awarded yesterday

words.note: essere plus stato, the auxiliary a past passive takes. It agrees with the subject: è stato for a man, è stata for a woman.
The past participle of premiare, from premio. It agrees with whoever won: premiata for her, premiato for him.

sentences.trap: Two agreements in one sentence, not one. stata agrees with madre and so does premiata — leave either as the -o form and you have written a man.
sentences.sound: eh STA-ta pre-MYA-ta: the two -ata endings chime, which is the agreement doing its work out loud.

variations.cue: My father was given the award
variations.changed: the masculine, with both endings moved

variations.cue: My mother was given the award

mistake.why: Both participles agree with madre, and madre is feminine. One -o ending is a slip; two of them says the sentence was assembled out of English.

sentences.usage: Reporting a ceremony, in speech or in a printed programme.

sentences.display: Egregio signore, carissimi amici, vorrei ringraziare
sentences.cue: Dear Sir, dearest friends, I would like to say thank you
sentences.literal: Distinguished sir, dearest friends, I-would-like to-thank

words.note: The opening of a formal letter to one named person. It is written rather than spoken, and it is far stiffer than the English Dear.
A warm opening to a group: the -issimo of caro, taught at L1-M10, in the plural. Warm where egregio is stiff.
The verb behind grazie (L1-M2). A speech says vorrei ringraziare rather than grazie, because a formula wants a whole clause.

sentences.trap: Do not open a letter with caro to somebody you have never met. caro is for people you know; a stranger with a title gets egregio, and the slip is visible on the page.
sentences.sound: e-GREH-jo, with a soft g. ca-RIS-see-mee, with the double s held. rin-gra-TSYA-re, the zi as ts.

variations.changed: the clause a speech actually begins with

mistake.why: caro to a stranger is too close. A formal letter opens Egregio, and caro waits until you know the person.

sentences.usage: The first line of a speech, or of a formal letter.
sentences.mnemonic: egregio for a stranger, carissimi for a room of friends.

sentences.display: Vorrei parlare a nome di mia madre, in qualità di figlia
sentences.cue: I would like to speak on my mother's behalf, as her daughter
sentences.literal: I-would-like to-speak at name of my mother, in quality of daughter

words.note: Learned whole. Literally in the name of: Italian uses a where English uses on, and no article comes between di and the person.
States the role you are speaking from. No article after di and none before qualità either — the whole phrase is frozen.

sentences.trap: in qualità di takes no article. in qualità di una figlia is the English a leaking through; the role is named bare.
sentences.sound: a NO-me dee. in kwa-li-TA dee, with the stress on the final a, which the accent marks.

variations.display: Vorrei parlare a nome di mia madre
variations.cue: I'd like to speak on my mother's behalf

mistake.display: Vorrei parlare in nome di una figlia
mistake.why: Two slips in one line: the phrase is a nome di and not in nome di, and in qualità di never takes an article after it.

sentences.usage: Standing up at a ceremony to speak for somebody who is not speaking.
sentences.mnemonic: a nome di says for whom; in qualità di says as what.

sentences.display: Poiché è tardi, il discorso è finito
sentences.cue: Since it is late, the speech is over
sentences.literal: Since is late, the speech is finished

words.note: A written since, giving a reason already accepted. Speech uses perché; the accent on the final e is where the stress falls.
A speech, the thing somebody stands up to give. Also a line of argument, much as English discourse can be.

sentences.trap: poiché is not perché. perché also answers a question — why? — and poiché never does; it only introduces a reason nobody is disputing.
sentences.sound: poy-KEH, stressed on the last syllable and the ch hard. dis-COR-so.

variations.display: Il discorso è finito, pertanto brindiamo
variations.cue: The speech is over, so let's toast
variations.changed: the conclusion carrying the other connective

mistake.display: Poiche è tardi, il discorso è finito
mistake.why: poiché carries an acute accent on the e, and without it the word is not a word. The accent also tells you the stress is on the end.

sentences.usage: Closing a speech, or writing one.
sentences.mnemonic: poiché opens the reason; pertanto closes it.

comprehensionPool.cue: My mother was given the award

comprehensionPool.display: Vorrei ringraziare a nome di mia madre
comprehensionPool.cue: I would like to thank you on my mother's behalf

comprehensionPool.display: Poiché è tardi, il discorso è finito
comprehensionPool.cue: Since it is late, the speech is over
